rules.title: California statewide rent cap (Tenant Protection Act, Civ. Code § 1947.12)
rules.requirement: Over any 12-month period, an owner of residential real property may not raise the gross rental rate for a dwelling or unit by more than 5% plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10%, whichever is lower. The base is the lowest gross rental rate charged in the prior 12 months, excluding discounts, incentives, concessions or credits the tenant accepted. The cost-of-living change uses the regional CPI-U named in the statute, rounded to the nearest 0.1%. If the same tenant remains, the rent may be raised in no more than two increments in 12 months. The owner may set the initial rent for a new tenancy when no prior tenant remains in lawful possession. Rent increase notices must follow Civ. Code § 827. A tenant may not sublease for more than the allowed rent. Waivers are void. An owner who collects excess rent is liable for injunctive relief, the overcharge, and attorney's fees. Willful, oppressive, fraudulent or malicious violations bring up to three times the overcharge. Suits must be filed within 3 years. The Attorney General, city attorney or county counsel may enforce.
rules.key_value: Lower of 5% + regional CPI change or 10% per 12 months; at most 2 increments per 12 months; overcharge damages, up to 3x if willful; 3-year limitations period; repealed Jan. 1, 2030

new_construction_exemption.basis: certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years (rolling); mobilehomes are not exempt on this basis

unverifiable_exemptions: Housing restricted by deed, regulatory agreement or recorded document as very low, low or moderate income affordable housing, or subject to an affordable housing subsidy agreement
Dormitories owned and operated by a higher education institution or a K-12 school

Separately alienable property (e.g. single-family home or condo) whose owner is not a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member or mobilehome park management, where the tenants received the statutory written exemption notice
Two units in a single structure where the owner occupied one unit as principal residence at the start of the tenancy and still does, and neither unit is an ADU or JADU
Housing under a valid local rent or price control that limits annual increases to less than this cap
coverage.summary: Residential dwellings and units statewide, including units in mobilehome parks. Exempt: housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years (rolling, except mobilehomes), deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing, dormitories, housing under a stricter local rent control, qualifying separately alienable property with the written notice, and owner-occupied duplexes. Homeowners of mobilehomes are not covered.
coverage.owner_conditions: The separately-alienable exemption applies only if the owner is not a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member or mobilehome park management, and the written exemption notice was given (in the rental agreement for tenancies commenced or renewed on or after July 1, 2020, or July 1, 2022 for mobilehomes). The owner-occupied duplex exemption lasts only while the owner continues in occupancy.
coverage.other_conditions: Under subd. (d)(3), housing subject to local rent control consistent with Civ. Code ch. 2.7 (§ 1954.50 et seq.) that limits annual increases below this cap is exempt, so stricter municipal rent control applies instead (e.g. rent-controlled units in Los Angeles, San Francisco, Berkeley and Santa Ana). The section does not expand or limit local authority under ch. 2.7.

rules.exemptions: Deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing; school and university dormitories; housing under a stricter local rent or price control; housing with a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years (except mobilehomes); separately alienable property with a qualifying non-corporate owner and written notice; owner-occupied duplex (no ADU/JADU); homeowners of mobilehomes.
rules.effective_date_note: The current version was repealed and re-added by Stats. 2023, ch. 290 (SB 567). It took effect Jan. 1, 2024 and became operative April 1, 2024 under subd. (n). Subd. (h) applies the cap to rent increases on or after March 15, 2019, and subd. (i) to mobilehome tenancies from Feb. 18, 2021. The section is repealed as of Jan. 1, 2030 (subd. (o)).
citation_aliases: Cal. Civ. Code ch. 2 (Hiring of Real Property)
rules.quoted_span: an owner of residential real property shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or a unit more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, of the lowest gross rental rate charged for that dwelling or unit at any time during the 12 months prior to the effective date of the increase.
rules.review_note: The statute publishes no annual percentage; the cap is computed per region from CPI-U. The LAHD page (last modified Sept. 2026) lists Los Angeles-area caps only through July 31, 2025 (8.9% for Aug. 1, 2024–Jul. 31, 2025; 8.8% for the prior year), so the current-year figure is not in the documents. Exemptions based on owner type and notice cannot be checked from an address.
rules.source_notes: Official statute text (D024). The LAHD page (D040) describes the same law as AB 1482 for Los Angeles. Its description of the duplex exemption (owner occupied the second unit 'for the entire period of the tenancy') is looser than the statute, which requires owner occupancy at the start of the tenancy, continued occupancy, and no ADU/JADU; the statute governs. The cell candidate quoted only the legislative findings in subd. (m) and is merged here.

also_supported_by.quoted_span: limited to no more than 5% plus the percentage change in the cost of living for the region in which the property is located, or 10% whichever is lower

rules.title: California Tenant Protection Act just-cause eviction (Civ. Code § 1946.2)
rules.requirement:
Once a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a unit for 12 months, the owner may terminate the tenancy only for just cause, stated in the written notice. If an adult tenant was added before an existing tenant reached 24 months, the rule applies only when all tenants have 12 months or one tenant has 24 months.

At-fault causes: nonpayment; breach of a material lease term; nuisance; waste; refusal to sign a similar lease extension; criminal activity or threats against the owner; unauthorized assignment or sublet; refusal of lawful entry; unlawful use; an employee or licensee failing to vacate; failure to deliver possession after the tenant's own notice.

No-fault causes: owner or relative move-in for at least 12 months, subject to lease-term conditions for leases from July 1, 2020; withdrawal from the rental market; a government, court or ordinance vacate order; demolition or substantial remodel requiring at least 30 consecutive days' vacancy.

Owner move-in rules:
- The notice must name the occupant and the relationship.
- The occupant must move in within 90 days and live there 12 months.
- Otherwise the owner must re-offer the unit to the tenant at the same terms and pay moving costs.

Remodel or demolition notices must contain specified statements and permits.

A curable violation requires a notice to cure before a 3-day notice to quit.

For a no-fault termination, the owner must either pay relocation equal to one month's rent within 15 calendar days of service or waive the final month's rent in writing, and must state this right in the notice.

Owners must give a prescribed notice of these rights. Non-compliance voids the termination notice. Material violations bring actual damages, discretionary attorney's fees, and up to treble damages plus punitive damages for willful conduct. Public enforcers may seek injunctions. Waivers are void.
rules.key_value: Applies after 12 months' occupancy (24 months if an adult tenant was added). No-fault relocation equal to 1 month's rent, paid within 15 calendar days, or a final-month rent waiver. Owner move-in: occupant must move in within 90 days and stay 12 months. Remodel requires at least 30 consecutive days' vacancy. Up to 3x damages for willful violations. Repealed Jan. 1, 2030.

new_construction_exemption.basis: certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years (rolling); not applicable to mobilehomes

unverifiable_exemptions: Housing restricted by deed, regulatory agreement or recorded document as very low, low or moderate income affordable housing, or subject to an affordable housing subsidy agreement
Separately alienable property whose owner is not a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member or mobilehome park management, where the tenant received the statutory written exemption notice
Single-family owner-occupied residence where the owner rents no more than two units or bedrooms (including ADU/JADU), or a mobilehome
Two units in one structure with the owner occupying one unit since the start of the tenancy (no ADU/JADU)
Tenant shares a bathroom or kitchen with an owner who lives on the property
Transient and tourist hotels; nonprofit hospital, religious, extended care, RCFE and adult residential facilities; school dormitories
Property covered by a local just-cause ordinance adopted on or before Sept. 1, 2019, or by a more protective later ordinance
coverage.summary: Residential real property statewide, including units in mobilehome parks, after 12 months of occupancy. Exempt: listed property types, housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years, and property covered by a qualifying local just-cause ordinance. Homeowners of mobilehomes are not covered.
coverage.owner_conditions: The separately-alienable exemption requires a non-REIT, non-corporate owner (or LLC with no corporate member, not mobilehome park management) and the written notice. Owner-occupancy exemptions last only while the owner keeps the unit as principal residence.
coverage.other_conditions: Under subd. (i), a local just-cause ordinance adopted on or before Sept. 1, 2019, or a later one that is more protective and contains a binding finding saying so, applies instead (e.g. the Los Angeles JCO/RSO, San Francisco Rent Ordinance, Berkeley ordinance, San Diego and Santa Ana ordinances, where they qualify). A property is never subject to both. A local ordinance adopted after Sept. 1, 2019 that is less protective is not enforced unless this section is repealed.

rules.exemptions: Transient and tourist hotels; nonprofit hospital, religious, extended care, RCFE and adult residential facilities; school dormitories; shared bath or kitchen with a resident owner; owner-occupied single-family residence renting at most two units or bedrooms; owner-occupied duplex; housing with a certificate of occupancy within 15 years (except mobilehomes); qualifying separately alienable property with notice; deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing; property under a qualifying local just-cause ordinance; homeowners of mobilehomes.
rules.effective_date_note: Subd. (m) makes this version operative April 1, 2024. The text as amended by Stats. 2025, ch. 203 (AB 1529) took effect Jan. 1, 2026. The section is repealed as of Jan. 1, 2030 (subd. (n)). The text refers to lease and notice dates of 2020 and 2022 (mobilehomes) but does not state when the original section first took effect.
citation_aliases: Cal. Civ. Code ch. 2 (Hiring of Real Property)
rules.quoted_span: after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy.
rules.review_note: Whether a given local ordinance qualifies under subd. (i) depends on its adoption date and on whether it contains a binding finding that it is more protective; check per city. Exemptions based on owner type and notice cannot be checked from an address.
rules.source_notes: Official statute text (D023). The relocation assistance and cure-notice rules in subds. (c)-(d), captured by the cell candidate, are part of the same section and are folded in here.

rules.title: Relocation payments for temporary capital improvement displacement under 20 days (Civ. Code § 1947.9)
rules.requirement: For temporary capital improvement evictions lasting less than 20 days, relocation payments are governed by Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.9 rather than S.F. Rent Ordinance § 37.9C. The San Francisco Rent Board lists a per-day payment per tenant household plus actual moving expenses, set by the date the eviction notice is served.
rules.key_value: Notices served 3/1/2026–2/28/2027: $446.00/day per tenant household plus actual moving expenses (3/1/2025–2/28/2026: $436.00/day)

coverage.summary: Temporary displacement of fewer than 20 days for capital improvement work. The only document is a San Francisco Rent Board rate page.
coverage.other_conditions: Per the SF Rent Board, this displaces the local § 37.9C relocation amounts for these short evictions.

rules.effective_date_note: The documents give no effective date for the statute. The $446.00/day rate applies to notices served March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027, and the rate is reset each March 1.
citation_aliases: Cal. Civ. Code ch. 2 (Hiring of Real Property)
rules.quoted_span: The amount of relocation payments for temporary capital improvement evictions for less than 20 days is governed by California Civil Code Section 1947.9 and not by Rent Ordinance Section 37.9C.
rules.review_note: The statute text of § 1947.9 is not among the documents. Its geographic scope and the basis for the daily rate cannot be verified; the rate is published by the San Francisco Rent Board, and applies_only_in is left null because the page does not say the statute is limited to San Francisco.
rules.source_notes: Official SF Rent Board rate report (D083).

rules.title: California residential security deposit cap, deductions and return (Civ. Code § 1950.5)
rules.requirement:
Cap and definition:
- Security, however denominated, may not exceed one month's rent in addition to first month's rent.
- Security includes any payment, fee, deposit or charge imposed at the start of a tenancy, including tenant-processing charges and advance rent. Screening fees under § 1950.6 are excluded.
- An advance payment of at least six months' rent is allowed on a lease of six months or more.
- A landlord who is a natural person (including a family-trust settlor or beneficiary) or an LLC whose members are all natural persons, and who owns no more than two residential rental properties with no more than four units offered for rent in total, may take up to two months' rent. This does not apply to a service member, and the landlord may not refuse to rent to a service member on that account.
- Higher security charged to service members must be explained in writing and the excess returned after six months without arrears.

Holding and deductions:
- Security is held for the tenant.
- Deductions are limited to amounts reasonably necessary for unpaid rent, damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, cleaning to the move-in level, and restoring personal property if the lease allows.

Inspections and photographs:
- The landlord must notify the tenant of the right to a pre-move-out inspection and perform it on request.
- The landlord must photograph the unit at move-in (tenancies beginning on or after July 1, 2025).
- The landlord must photograph the unit after possession returns and after repairs (from April 1, 2025).

Return:
- Within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates, the landlord must return the balance with an itemized statement, invoices or receipts, and photographs.
- Documentation is not required for deductions of $125 or less, or if the tenant waived it, unless the tenant requests it within 14 days.
- Security received electronically must be returned electronically unless otherwise agreed.

Other rules and penalties:
- Successors in interest are liable if the security is not properly transferred.
- Security may not be called 'nonrefundable'.
- Bad-faith retention brings statutory damages of up to twice the security plus actual damages.
rules.key_value: Cap of 1 month's rent (2 months for qualifying small landlords, never for service members); return with itemized statement within 21 calendar days; documentation waived at $125 or less unless requested; bad-faith damages up to 2x the security

unverifiable_exemptions: Small-landlord two-month cap: landlord is a natural person (including a family-trust settlor or beneficiary) or an LLC whose members are all natural persons, and owns no more than two residential rental properties with no more than four units offered for rent in total
coverage.landlord_size_condition: The two-month cap applies only to a natural person or an all-natural-person LLC owning no more than two residential rental properties with no more than four dwelling units offered for rent collectively, and never to a service member tenant.
coverage.summary: Security for any rental agreement for residential property used as the tenant's dwelling, statewide.
coverage.owner_conditions: Small-landlord ownership structure determines whether the higher two-month cap is available.
coverage.other_conditions: The cap in subd. (c) does not apply to security collected or demanded before July 1, 2024. Initial-inspection duties do not apply to terminations under CCP § 1161(2)-(4). Local deposit-interest rules (e.g. Berkeley, Los Angeles RSO, San Francisco) are complementary.

rules.exemptions: Advance payment of at least six months' rent on a lease of six months or more; tenant-requested paid alterations; the two-month small-landlord cap is unavailable for service members; itemized documentation not required for deductions of $125 or less or if waived, unless the tenant requests it.
rules.effective_date_note: The one-month cap applies to security collected or demanded on or after July 1, 2024 (subd. (c)(6)). Later dates: service-member provisions on or after April 1, 2025; move-out photographs from April 1, 2025; move-in photographs for tenancies beginning on or after July 1, 2025. The current text was amended by Stats. 2025, ch. 340 (AB 414), effective Jan. 1, 2026. Before July 1, 2024 the caps were two months' rent unfurnished and three months furnished (per Berkeley Rent Board).
citation_aliases: Cal. Civ. Code ch. 2 (Hiring of Real Property)
rules.quoted_span: Except as provided in paragraph (2), (3), or (5), a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.
rules.review_note: Whether a landlord qualifies for the two-month cap depends on ownership facts that cannot be checked from an address. The Berkeley Rent Board says it cannot determine this for a new tenancy.
rules.source_notes: Official statute text (D025). The Berkeley Rent Board page (D007) describes the AB 12 change. It says the small landlord owns 'only two' properties where the statute says 'no more than two', and it omits the service-member exception; the statute governs. D007's statement that proof of completed repairs is required from Jan. 1, 2025 is not dated in the current statute text, which requires invoices and receipts and photographs.

also_supported_by.quoted_span: Starting July 1, 2024, many landlords may only charge one month's rent for unfurnished and furnished units

rules.title: California application screening fee cap, receipt and refund rules (Civ. Code § 1950.6)
rules.requirement:
Fee cap:
- A landlord or agent may charge an applicant (including a guarantor or cosigner) a screening fee only for actual out-of-pocket costs of gathering information, including screening or credit-report services and the reasonable value of time.
- The fee may never exceed $30 per applicant, adjustable annually by the landlord with the CPI from Jan. 1, 1998.
- No fee may be charged when the landlord knows or should know that no unit is or will soon be available.

Allowed screening processes. A fee may be charged only if the landlord offers one of these:
- (A) Completed applications are considered in the order received under written criteria given with the application. The first qualified applicant is approved. No fee is charged until the application is actually considered. Fees collected inadvertently from concurrent applications are refunded within 7 days, or applied to another unit at the applicant's option.
- (B) The entire fee is returned to every applicant not selected within 7 days of selection or 30 days of application, whichever comes first.

Other duties:
- The landlord must give an itemized receipt (email by agreement).
- The landlord must return any unused fee if no reference check or credit report is obtained.
- The landlord must give the applicant a copy of the credit report within 7 days of receiving it.
- Reusable screening reports under § 1950.1 may be accepted.
- The fee is not 'security' under § 1950.5.
rules.key_value: $30 per applicant base, CPI-adjustable annually since Jan. 1, 1998 (Berkeley Rent Board lists $68.96 as the 2026 maximum); itemized receipt; credit report copy within 7 days; refund within 7 days of selection or 30 days of application (whichever first) under option (B)

coverage.summary: Owners of residential rental property and their agents charging application screening fees to applicants, guarantors or cosigners, statewide.
coverage.other_conditions: Not intended to preempt rules governing deposits and fees under federal or state housing assistance programs. Berkeley adds a local disclosure duty (BMC 13.78.010) that is complementary.

rules.exemptions: No refund owed to an applicant denied after consideration for failing the established criteria under option (A); federal and state housing assistance program fee rules are not preempted.
rules.effective_date_note: Effective date of the current text as amended by Stats. 2025, ch. 67 (AB 1170). The $30 cap predates this amendment (CPI adjustment runs from Jan. 1, 1998). The documents do not state when the cap first took effect.
citation_aliases: Cal. Civ. Code ch. 2 (Hiring of Real Property)
rules.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant.
rules.conflict_note: Open question: there is no single official statewide 2026 dollar figure for the cap. The statute sets a $30 base that the landlord may adjust by CPI. The Berkeley Rent Board (a city body) publishes $68.96 as the 2026 maximum, but no state-published figure appears in the documents.
rules.review_note: The statute leaves the CPI adjustment to the landlord and does not name the index or a published amount; treat $68.96 as a Berkeley Rent Board figure.
rules.source_notes: Official statute text (D026). The public.law mirror (DX08) reproduces the same text but omits clause (c)(2)(A)(iii). The Berkeley Rent Board page (D005) summarizes the same rules for 2026.

also_supported_by.quoted_span: Prospective tenants should expect to receive a copy of their credit report within 7 days of receipt by the landlord
In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant.

rules.title: California FEHA housing discrimination: source of income and subsidized-applicant screening (Gov. Code § 12955)
rules.requirement:
Owners of housing accommodations may not discriminate against or harass anyone because of source of income, among other protected characteristics. Ads and notices may not indicate a source-of-income preference. Source of income means lawful, verifiable income paid to the tenant or to the landlord on the tenant's behalf, including public assistance and housing subsidies such as Section 8 and HUD-VASH vouchers.

Income standards must count the aggregate income of persons residing together on the same basis as married persons.

Where there is a government rent subsidy:
- Income standards must be based on the tenant's portion of the rent.
- An owner who uses credit history must offer the applicant the option of lawful, verifiable alternative evidence of ability to pay (such as benefit payments, pay records or bank statements).
- The owner must allow reasonable time to respond and must reasonably consider that evidence in lieu of credit history.

Owners may still ask about the level or source of income, verify employment, request landlord references and verify identity. Per the CRD, refusing Section 8 vouchers, refusing to complete subsidy paperwork, and 'No Section 8' ads are discrimination.
rules.key_value: Source of income (including Section 8 and HUD-VASH vouchers) is a protected class; income standards based on the tenant's portion of rent where subsidized; alternative evidence must be offered in lieu of credit history for subsidized applicants

coverage.summary: Owners of any housing accommodation in California. The subsidy-specific income-standard and credit-history rules apply only where there is a government rent subsidy.
coverage.owner_conditions: Per the CRD FAQ (not the statute text): an owner-occupant renting to one additional person may exclude applicants on protected characteristics but may not publish discriminatory statements or ads.
coverage.other_conditions: Per the CRD FAQ: shared living areas may be limited to one sex, and qualifying senior housing may be limited by age.

rules.exemptions: Inquiry into the level or source of income is not discrimination (subd. (p)(2)); verification of employment, landlord references and identity remain allowed (subd. (o)(2)).
rules.effective_date_note: Effective date of the current text as amended by Stats. 2023, ch. 776 (SB 267), which added the subsidized-applicant credit-history rule. Per the California Apartment Association (secondary), the Section 8 / housing-subsidy part of source of income (SB 329) has applied since Jan. 1, 2020.
rules.quoted_span: (a) For the owner of any housing accommodation to discriminate against or harass any person because of the race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income, disability, veteran or military status, or genetic information of that person.
rules.review_note: Only the source-of-income and screening parts of this multi-class section are captured. The FEHA exemptions for owner-occupants, single-sex shared space and senior housing come from the CRD FAQ, not this section's text. Local source-of-income or screening ordinances are complementary.
rules.source_notes: Official statute text (D027). The CAA article (DX07) calls SB 267 'last year's' without a date; the official code footer identifies it as Stats. 2023, ch. 776, effective Jan. 1, 2024, so the '(2024)' label in candidate DX07:c3 is resolved. SB 329 (DX07:c2) and SB 267 (DX07:c3) both amended this source-of-income framework and are merged here despite low text similarity.

also_supported_by.quoted_span: Refusing to rent to a tenant with a section 8 voucher.
This change meant that, as of Jan. 1, 2020, state law prohibits landlords from refusing to participate in such programs.
SB 267 amended FEHA to prohibit rental property owners from using a person’s credit history as part of the application process

rules.title: California Civil Rights Council regulations on criminal history in housing decisions
rules.requirement:
Housing providers, including tenant screening companies, may check an applicant's criminal history, but with limits:
- They may not consider arrests that did not lead to conviction, sealed or expunged records, or juvenile justice records.
- Blanket bans on people with any criminal history are prohibited.
- A denial based on a conviction must be directly related to the applicant's ability to be a good tenant and not a threat to the health and safety of others and the property.
- Providers should weigh the nature and severity of the crime and the time elapsed since it.

The regulations also limit what criminal history may be sought and what actions may be taken on it.
rules.key_value: No blanket bans; arrests without conviction, sealed or expunged records and juvenile records may not be considered; denials must be directly related to tenancy; in effect since Jan. 1, 2020

coverage.summary: Most housing providers and housing-related services in California covered by FEHA, including landlords, property managers and tenant screening companies.
coverage.other_conditions: Stricter local rules (e.g. Berkeley's Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance, which bars asking about criminal history at all) operate alongside these limits.

rules.effective_date_note: Per the CAA (secondary), the Civil Rights Council (formerly the Fair Employment and Housing Council) adopted the regulations in 2019 and they took effect Jan. 1, 2020. The CRD page gives no date.
citation_aliases: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 2, § 12264 et seq.
Civil Rights Council criminal history regulations
Fair Employment and Housing Council regulations
rules.quoted_span: Housing  providers cannot consider some types of criminal history including arrests that did not lead to a conviction, records that are sealed or expunged, or records or matters processed in the juvenile justice system.
rules.review_note: Neither the CRD page nor the CAA article cites a regulation section. The § 12264 citation is not stated in any document and must be verified against the regulation text, which is not captured.
rules.source_notes: The official CRD fair housing page and FAQ (D016) describe these protections under FEHA. The CAA compliance reminder (DX07, secondary) identifies them as Civil Rights Council regulations effective Jan. 1, 2020. The source-of-income part of D016:c1 is covered by the Gov. Code § 12955 record.

also_supported_by.quoted_span: Blanket bans on applicants with a criminal record are prohibited, as are policies that consider arrests without convictions.

rules.title: California Cartwright Act: common pricing algorithm prohibition (AB 325)
rules.requirement:
It is unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce. It is also unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm while coercing another person to set or adopt its recommended price or commercial term for the same or similar products or services in California.

Definitions:
- A common pricing algorithm is any methodology, including a computer, software or other technology, used by two or more persons, that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set or otherwise influence a price or commercial term.
- Commercial term includes level of service, availability and output.
- Distribution includes selling, licensing, providing access or subscriptions.
- Person excludes the end consumer.

The statute is a general antitrust rule and does not mention housing; it reaches rent-setting software through its general terms. The companion § 16756.1 lets a Cartwright Act complaint plead only facts making a conspiracy plausible, without excluding independent action. Per the secondary source, single-firm algorithms using only the business's own data are not covered.
rules.key_value: Use or distribution of a common pricing algorithm in a conspiracy, or with coercion, is unlawful. The violation is a Cartwright Act violation, which the bill digest says is punishable as a crime. Per secondary source (separate SB 763 amendments): criminal fines up to the greater of $6M (corporations) / $1M (individuals) or twice the gain or loss; civil penalties up to $1M per violation in AG/DA actions; treble damages in private suits.

coverage.summary: Any person (as defined in Bus. & Prof. Code § 16702, excluding end consumers) who uses or distributes a common pricing algorithm, in any industry including residential rentals; not limited by building characteristics.
coverage.other_conditions: The algorithm must be used by two or more persons and must use competitor data.

rules.exemptions: End consumers are excluded from 'person'. Per the secondary source, proprietary algorithms using only a business's own data are not covered.
rules.effective_date_note: Approved by the Governor and filed with the Secretary of State Oct. 6, 2025 (Stats. 2025, ch. 338). The bill text states no operative date. The Jan. 1, 2026 effective date comes from the Cleary Gottlieb alert (DX09).
citation_aliases: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16700 et seq.
rules.quoted_span: (a) It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.
rules.review_note: The penalty amounts rest on a secondary description of separate amendments (SB 763, §§ 16755, 16755.1) whose text is not captured. Subd. (c) preserves other antitrust laws, and the text says nothing about local ordinances. Local rent-algorithm bans (Berkeley ch. 13.63, S.F. Admin. Code § 37.10C, Santa Ana; San Diego's is pending) appear to operate alongside this statute, but the documents do not address their interaction.
rules.source_notes: Official chaptered bill text (D022). The law-firm alert (DX09) and the cell candidate describe the same provisions and are merged here.

also_supported_by.quoted_span: As of January 1, 2026, businesses are subject to the Cartwright Act’s latest amendments, including an express prohibition on certain usages of pricing algorithms.
The Cartwright Act now expressly prohibits (1) using or distributing common algorithms to collude on pricing, and (2) coercing users to adopt algorithmic recommendations.

dropped_candidates.reason: Gov. Code § 12955(f) is the fair-housing anti-retaliation clause, not a just-cause eviction rule (no allowed causes, notice or relocation). Out of scope for just_cause_eviction; § 12955 is kept as a screening_restrictions record.

known_gaps.law: SB 763 (2025) – Cartwright Act penalties, Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 16755, 16755.1
